Post-endodontic pain

PBM may reduce pain after some root-canal procedures, but recent randomized studies report both positive and null results.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

PBM may reduce pain after some root-canal procedures, but recent randomized studies report both positive and null results.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact endodontic-postoperative category contains 33 unique titles: 22 human randomized reports, one nonrandomized study, one rat study, eight reviews or syntheses, and one protocol. Reviews overlap the primary trials. Laser-activated irrigation is excluded unless the record specifically tests PBM, because it is a different intervention. (Freitas-Júnior et al. 2026 Reddy et al. 2026)

Human and clinical evidence

The clinical results are mixed. Freitas-Júnior et al. randomized 70 patients receiving emergency pulpectomy and found no overall treatment effect on pain; isolated time-point scores were higher in the PBM group. Reddy et al. randomized 80 single-visit root-canal patients and reported lower pain and analgesic use with PBM. These studies address different diagnoses and care settings, and the positive result needs independent replication.

Animal evidence

One rat study is indexed. It does not determine the effect of PBM on postoperative pain in endodontic patients.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate in-vitro or ex-vivo study is identified in this exact symptom category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Both recent trials used 808 nm near-infrared diode lasers. Reddy et al. reported 4 J/cm² for 40 seconds in one postoperative session. Freitas-Júnior et al. used 100 mW continuous emission immediately after treatment; a comparable fluence was not provided in the abstract. Diagnosis, laser placement, dose, and analgesic care differ between studies.

Interpretation

There is no consistent effect estimate across acute endodontic pain settings. Future trials should stratify by pulpal and periapical diagnosis, preregister protocols, report fluence and application points, and assess pain and analgesic consumption at common intervals. Adequate blinding and replication are needed before routine use can be supported.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for acute post-endodontic pain. Randomized trials conflict: a recent emergency-care trial was null overall, while another trial reported benefit.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains 33 unique titles, including 22 randomized reports and eight reviews or syntheses. Pain timing, diagnoses, treatment protocols, and co-interventions differ. A 2026 emergency pulpectomy trial found no overall benefit, whereas another trial reported lower pain and analgesic use. Replication with common outcomes is needed.
